questions.stem: On the JDK's default providers, a batch job encrypts invoice lines of one fixed length with `Cipher.getInstance("AES")` and a call to `init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` before each line, and stores the output. Two lines have identical text. What does someone reading the stored column without the key see?

options.text: Identical stored bytes for the two lines, since each init call sets up a cipher that uses nothing but the key
options.says: SunJCE's default for "AES" is ECB, which has no IV, so equal blocks give equal ciphertext blocks

options.text: Identical stored bytes for the two lines, since init with no parameters reuses the IV of the line before
options.says: ECB uses no IV at all (getIV() returns null); the repeat comes from the mode, not from a reused IV

options.text: Different stored bytes for the two lines, since init with no parameters draws a fresh IV for each line
options.says: only a mode that takes an IV, such as GCM, draws one; "AES" means ECB, which takes none

options.text: Different stored bytes for the two lines, since each init call starts the cipher over with fresh internal state
options.says: under ECB a re-init with the same key changes nothing: the same block and key always give the same output block

origin.section: Cipher.getInstance("AES") Is ECB, and ECB Encrypts Equal Blocks to Equal Blocks

questions.stem: A service draws a 12-byte GCM IV from `SecureRandom` once, at start-up. It creates a new `Cipher` for every message, and seals thousands of messages a day under one key. What does someone who holds two of the stored ciphertexts, but not the key, learn from them?

options.text: The XOR of the two plaintexts, since the same key and IV produce the same keystream for both
options.says: XOR-ing the two ciphertexts cancels the shared keystream and leaves the XOR of the plaintexts

options.text: Each of the two plaintexts, since the same key and IV let each one be decrypted on its own
options.says: the repeat yields only the plaintexts' XOR; reading one message needs the other one known first

options.text: Only that the IV repeated, since the second seal throws InvalidAlgorithmParameterException for the repeated IV
options.says: SunJCE refuses a repeated key and IV only on the same Cipher object; a new Cipher accepts them

options.text: Only that the IV repeated, since an IV drawn from SecureRandom keeps the two keystreams unrelated
options.says: how the IV was drawn doesn't matter once it is used twice; the keystream depends only on key and IV

origin.section: A GCM IV Used Twice Under One Key Gives Away the XOR of the Two Plaintexts

questions.stem: A team replaces unsalted SHA-256 password digests with SHA-256 over a random 16-byte per-user salt followed by the password. Later the users table leaks. For an attacker after one particular user's password, what is true now?

options.text: Each guess still costs one SHA-256, since the salt changes which digests match but not the work per guess
options.says: a guess is still one SHA-256 over salt and password; only an iteration count makes each guess cost more

options.text: Each guess now costs many SHA-256 rounds, since the salt changes the work per guess but not which digests match
options.says: the salt adds no rounds; the work per guess comes from an iteration count, which plain SHA-256 doesn't have

options.text: Each guess can use a precomputed digest table, since the salt changes neither the work per guess nor which digests match
options.says: a per-user salt makes equal passwords give different digests, so tables computed without that salt don't match

options.text: Each guess must start by recovering the salt, since the salt changes which digests match and is stored apart from them
options.says: the salt is not secret; it is stored beside the hash, so a leaked table includes it

origin.section: A Password Hash Needs a Salt per User and a Slow Function: PBKDF2, Not SHA-256

questions.stem: An API checks request signatures with `Arrays.equals(computedTag, receivedTag)`, where computedTag is the 32-byte HMAC it computed and receivedTag is whatever the request carried, decoded. A reviewer asks for `MessageDigest.isEqual(computedTag, receivedTag)` instead. What does the change alter?

options.text: How long a rejection takes, since the old check returns as soon as it finds a difference
options.says: Arrays.equals returns once it finds a difference; isEqual's time depends only on the length of its first argument

options.text: How long a rejection takes, since the new check returns as soon as it finds a length difference
options.says: the isEqual javadoc says its time does not depend on the length of the second argument

options.text: Which tags are accepted, since the old check also accepts a tag cut short to its first 16 bytes
options.says: both checks returned false for a 16-byte prefix of the tag

options.text: Which tags are accepted, since the old check throws on a missing tag where the new one returns false
options.says: both checks returned false for a null tag; neither threw

origin.section: Compare Tags and Hashes with MessageDigest.isEqual; Arrays.equals Stops at the First Difference
